headline: High risk of data leakage and cascading errors: both agents share filesystem/MCP/network surfaces, and nullclaw’s CRM-style data handling can amplify Goose outputs into sensitive downstream actions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read/write the filesystem and use MCP, so a shared workspace or MCP bridge can carry attacker-controlled content between them. Goose explicitly supports MCP and filesystem access; nullclaw also exposes workspace files and multiple channels. This is not proven by direct evidence, but the interaction pathway is plausible in default setups.
conditions: IF Goose and nullclaw are pointed at the same workspace or MCP server, injected instructions can cross from one agent to the other.
IF either agent parses file or MCP content as trusted instructions, prompt injection becomes actionable.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Disable shared MCP servers for one side.
Require provenance tags on all inter-agent messages.
Add a manual review step before executing file-derived instructions.
requires-engineering: enforce content sanitization on shared channels.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Goose touches source code and files in cwd, while nullclaw handles API keys, private keys, bearer tokens, conversation history, and workspace files. Both have filesystem access and broad network egress, so sensitive data can flow from shared files into outputs or remote APIs. The blast radius includes secrets exfiltration and workspace leakage.
conditions: IF both agents share any directory containing secrets or credentials, those secrets can be read by either agent.
IF nullclaw forwards workspace or conversation context to external services, sensitive Goose-managed files can leave the local environment.
mitigations: Move secrets out of any shared workspace.
Rotate credentials before pairing.
Restrict network egress for one agent.
Use separate OS users or containers.
requires-engineering: add per-file allowlists for uploads and context ingestion.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem, modify git state, spawn subprocesses, and use broad network egress. Goose shares state via filesystem across instances, and nullclaw uses durable memory plus workspace files, so concurrent writes can collide and corrupt repos or shared artifacts. The overlap is direct and dangerous by default.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git checkout, concurrent commits or file edits can conflict.
IF either agent runs package installs or subprocesses in the shared tree, state corruption can occur.
mitigations: Assign separate repositories per agent.
Pause one agent during the other's write phase.
Use git locks or a single-writer policy.
Snapshot the workspace before concurrent runs.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking for shared mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Goose can generate code, shell actions, and MCP-driven outputs; nullclaw has scheduling, webhook, and CRM-style automation surfaces that can act on those outputs. If nullclaw treats Goose output as authoritative, mistakes can cascade into emails, webhooks, or other downstream actions. The pairwise pathway is plausible and the blast radius is multi-step and potentially irreversible.
conditions: IF nullclaw consumes Goose output without verification, erroneous facts can be operationalized.
IF nullclaw schedules or triggers actions from Goose-generated text, downstream side effects can propagate.
mitigations: Require human approval before any outbound action.
Insert a verification step between agents.
Limit Goose output to structured, machine-checkable fields.
Disable auto-scheduling for paired runs.
requires-engineering: add confidence gating before webhooks or CRM actions.

E_compliance.rationale: Goose is documented as on-machine coding/ops software, while nullclaw touches audit logs, conversation history, memory, and sensitive tokens. If regulated or personal data is placed in the shared workspace, differing retention and logging behaviors can create compliance mismatch. The profiles do not prove a specific residency breach, so medium is the cautious choice.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in the shared workspace, retention and logging differences can create policy mismatch.
IF either agent exports logs or memory outside the intended jurisdiction, compliance obligations may be violated.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared folders.
Disable verbose logging for paired runs.
Review retention settings before use.
Separate personal and regulated workloads.
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls for both agents.
